title: Discrimination rules and automated decisions

sources.claim: New York City Local Law 144 (enforced from July 5, 2023): employers and employment agencies may use an automated employment decision tool only after an independent bias audit within the past year, with a public summary and advance notice to candidates.

Illinois HB 3773 amended the Illinois Human Rights Act, effective January 1, 2026: employers may not use AI in a way that discriminates against protected classes, may not use ZIP codes as a proxy for protected classes, and must give notice when AI is used for covered employment decisions.

Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9: a creditor taking adverse action must give a statement of the specific principal reasons, or tell the applicant how to request them. CFPB Circular 2023-03 (September 2023), which applied this to complex algorithms, was withdrawn on May 12, 2025 in a batch of 67 guidance documents; withdrawing guidance does not repeal the regulation.

jurisdiction: US (Illinois); US (New York City); US federal
effective_year: 2023; 2026; Regulation B in force; circular 2023, withdrawn 2025

sections.skill: Compare AI decision rules with a referee using instant replay

questions.prompt: Do the game's rules still apply with replay?

choices.text: No, because using technology replaces every rule that applied to the game before it

questions.intro: In some sports, referees use INSTANT REPLAY technology. The technology helps, but the rules of the game still apply, the referee is still responsible for the call, and teams can ask why a call was made. If a replay system were set up to favor one team, that would still be unfair, even though "the machine showed it." AI in hiring or lending is similar: the tool helps, but rules, responsibility and explanations remain.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for the call?

sections.skill: Track shared themes and changing guidance

questions.prompt: Which themes do these rules share?

choices.text: Testing for bias, notice and explaining decisions
Banning computers from workplaces and requiring all decisions to be made on paper by hand

questions.correct_answer: Testing for bias, notice and explaining decisions
questions.intro: These rules share themes: test for bias, tell people when automated tools are used, and be able to explain decisions. Details and coverage differ by place and sector, and agency guidance can be revised or withdrawn, so check the current status. "The algorithm decided" is not a defense that removes responsibility from the organization using it. People affected can ask what was used and why, and may have rights to complain or appeal.

questions.prompt: CFPB Circular 2023-03, which stressed this rule, was withdrawn on May 12, 2025. Did that remove Regulation B's reasons requirement?

Yes; withdrawing guidance cancels the regulation
